title: Indians Took 70% of H-1B Approvals as New-Employment Approvals Fell
excerpt: USCIS approved 406,348 H-1B petitions in fiscal 2025; Indian-born beneficiaries received 283,772, while initial-employment approvals dropped to 114,806 and renewals carried the program.
body:
• Indian-born professionals received 283,772 of the 406,348 H-1B petitions USCIS approved in fiscal 2025 — about 70% of the total, the largest share of any country.
  • Approvals for initial (new) employment fell to 114,806, while continuing-employment approvals — extensions, amendments and employer changes — held at 291,542.
  • Computer-related jobs accounted for 62% of approvals; median pay for approved beneficiaries was about $133,000, and about $140,000 in computer roles.
  • For readers: most approved petitions are renewals, not new visas — check your employer's filings in the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub, and note certain new petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the US carry a $100,000 payment under the presidential proclamation.

Indian-born professionals accounted for roughly seven in ten H-1B approvals in fiscal year 2025, even as approvals for new employment declined, according to USCIS data reported this week. USCIS approved 406,348 H-1B petitions in the year, of which 283,772 went to beneficiaries born in India. China was a distant second.

The composition of those approvals matters more than the headline total. Petitions for initial employment — the category covering new hires, largely subject to the annual cap of 65,000 plus 20,000 for holders of US advanced degrees — fell to 114,806. Continuing employment, covering extensions, amended petitions and changes of employer for people already in the United States, accounted for 291,542 approvals. The system is now dominated by people already working in the country renewing their status, not by new arrivals.

A Technology Program in Practice

Computer-related occupations made up 62% of all approvals, and systems analysis and programming alone represented about half. Median annual compensation for approved beneficiaries was around $133,000, rising to about $140,000 for computer-related roles. That pay profile is one reason analysts say senior, higher-paid engineers are better positioned under newer selection approaches that weight wages, while early-career applicants and lower-wage staffing models face a harder path.

The employer mix is shifting as well. An analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy, reported by Mint, found the seven largest India-based IT firms together won just 4,573 initial-employment approvals in FY2025 — down 37% from the previous year and about 70% below their FY2015 level. Only three India-based firms ranked among the top 25 employers for initial approvals. Amazon led all employers with 4,644 initial approvals, followed by Meta Platforms with 1,555, Microsoft with 1,394 and Google with 1,050. Across the economy, 28,277 US employers had at least one new H-1B approval; most were small users, with 61% approved for a single petition.

"The numbers show Indian-based companies now deliver IT services to US businesses using relatively few H-1B visas, while the largest US technology companies are hiring many individuals."

— Stuart Anderson, Executive Director, National Foundation for American Policy

What This Means for Indian Professionals

Denial rates remain low by historical standards: 2.8% for initial-employment petitions and 1.9% for continuing employment in FY2025, according to the NFAP analysis. The bigger change is cost and selection at the front end. USCIS guidance on H-1B specialty occupations sets out the $100,000 payment applying to certain petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the United States without a valid H-1B visa, alongside the existing registration and cap process. Employers' filing history can be reviewed through the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub, which covers decisions from fiscal 2009 onward.

For the diaspora, the practical read is twofold. Workers already in the US on H-1B status sit inside the larger, steadier continuing-employment stream, where approvals remain high. Aspiring applicants outside that stream — especially new graduates and candidates sponsored through high-volume services firms — face a smaller initial-employment pool, fewer approvals at the traditional Indian IT majors, and a selection system that increasingly rewards advanced US degrees and higher salaries.

What to Watch Next

The next test is the FY2027 cap season and how registrations respond to the new fee and wage-weighted selection. If initial approvals fall again while continuing approvals hold, the program's centre of gravity will keep moving from new entry toward retention — a shift with direct consequences for Indian students choosing US universities and for employers deciding whether roles are filled onshore or delivered from India.
